summary.text: The list contains \((1,2,1,1)\) but omits \((2,1,1,1)\). Interchanging the two square variables shows that these forms represent exactly the same integers, so they cannot have opposite full-representability classifications.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R(a,b,c,d)
\]
denote the assertion that \(a,b,c,d\) are positive integers and that every nonnegative integer \(n\) has a representation
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4
\]
with \(x,y,z,w\ge 0\).

The conjecture asserts, simultaneously for all positive coefficient quadruples, that \(R(a,b,c,d)\) holds if and only if \((a,b,c,d)\) belongs to the displayed list of 49 quadruples. We prove that this assertion is internally inconsistent with the symmetry between its two square terms.

First observe the following general symmetry. For any coefficients \(a,b,c,d\),
\[
R(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R(b,a,c,d).
\]
Indeed, positivity is unchanged when \(a\) and \(b\) are interchanged. Now assume \(R(a,b,c,d)\), and let \(n\ge 0\) be arbitrary. There are nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\) such that
\[
ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4=n.
\]
Set
\[
X=y,\qquad Y=x,\qquad Z=z,\qquad W=w.
\]
These new variables are still nonnegative, and, using commutativity of addition,
\[
\begin{aligned}
bX^2+aY^2+cZ^3+dW^4
 &=by^2+ax^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
 &=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
 &=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every \(n\) is represented after swapping the two square coefficients. Applying the same argument in reverse also shows that \(R(a,b,c,d)\) and \(R(b,a,c,d)\) are equivalent, although only the forward implication is needed.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the conjectured characterization by the displayed list is true.

The quadruple
\[
(1,2,1,1)
\]
is explicitly the first member of the proposed list. Therefore the “if” direction of the conjecture implies
\[
R(1,2,1,1).
\]
Concretely, the conjecture consequently says that the coefficients are positive and that, for every nonnegative integer \(n\), there are nonnegative \(x,y,z,w\) satisfying
\[
x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4=n.
\]

Use the square-term symmetry just established. Given such a representation of an arbitrary \(n\), interchange \(x\) and \(y\). If
\[
X=y,\qquad Y=x,
\]
then
\[
2X^2+Y^2+z^3+w^4
 =2y^2+x^2+z^3+w^4
 =x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4
 =n.
\]
All four coefficients \(2,1,1,1\) are positive. Hence
\[
R(2,1,1,1)
\]
holds.

The “only if” direction of the conjecture would now force
\[
(2,1,1,1)
\]
to occur in the proposed list. It does not. To check this directly, any list entry equal to \((2,1,1,1)\) would have to have fourth coordinate \(1\). The entries in the displayed list whose fourth coordinate is \(1\) are exactly
\[
\begin{gathered}
(1,2,1,1),\ (1,3,1,1),\ (1,6,1,1),\ (2,3,1,1),\ (2,4,1,1),\\
(1,1,2,1),\ (1,4,2,1),\ (1,2,3,1),\ (1,2,4,1),\ (1,2,12,1).
\end{gathered}
\]
Among the first five, whose third coordinate is \(1\), the two entries with first coordinate \(2\) have second coordinate \(3\) or \(4\), not \(1\); the other three have first coordinate \(1\). The remaining five already have third coordinate different from \(1\). Thus none is \((2,1,1,1)\). Every later entry in the proposed list has fourth coordinate at least \(2\), so none of those can equal \((2,1,1,1)\) either.

We have therefore derived both that \((2,1,1,1)\) must belong to the list and that it does not belong to the list. This contradiction disproves the conjecture.

The underlying defect is that any correct classification must be closed under swapping the coefficients of the two terms having the same exponent, \(ax^2\) and \(by^2\). The proposed classification is not closed under this symmetry: it includes \((1,2,1,1)\) but excludes \((2,1,1,1)\). No independent proof that \(x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4\) actually represents every nonnegative integer is needed for the disproof: under the conjecture itself, membership of \((1,2,1,1)\) supplies that assertion, and symmetry then yields the contradiction with the conjecture’s “only if” direction.
